clue.text: With them it is always the close season

definitions.text: With them it is always the close season

parts.words: With them it is always the close season
parts.note: a close season is when hunting is banned, but 'close' also means tight-fisted, so these people are always close with money

explanation.surface: A remark about anglers or hunters who never get to fish or shoot.
explanation.walkthrough: A close season in field sports is the period when game may not be taken; here 'close' means mean with money, so for misers every season is close.
explanation.definitionFit: Misers are stingy people, and 'close' is an old word for stingy.

clue.text: The philosopher is not old and not backward

parts.note: something that is not old is new

indicators.note: backward tells us the second 'not' is read from right to left

parts.note: the word taken as written

explanation.surface: A description of a thinker who is neither aged nor slow-witted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backward' turns NOT into TON. Isaac Newton's own term for his science was natural philosophy, which is why he is called a philosopher.
explanation.definitionFit: Isaac Newton wrote on natural philosophy, the old name for physics, so he counts as a philosopher.

clue.text: He was, no doubt, chiefly concerned with the Spanish question

definitions.text: He was, no doubt, chiefly concerned with the Spanish question

parts.words: He was, no doubt, chiefly concerned with the Spanish question
parts.note: 'chiefly' points to the head official, and 'question' to interrogation by the Spanish Inquisition

explanation.surface: A historian's remark about someone preoccupied with Spanish politics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Spanish question' sounds like a diplomatic problem, but it means the questioning of suspects by the Spanish Inquisition, and 'chiefly' makes him its head.
explanation.definitionFit: Torquemada and his successors led the Inquisition in Spain, putting heretics to interrogation.

clue.text: Ah ! so prim and concise, as the saying goes

indicators.note: goes suggests the letters of 'Ah' and 'so prim' moving off into a new order

explanation.surface: A prim person sighs out a neat little proverb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes' looks like part of the phrase 'as the saying goes', but it shuffles AH SO PRIM.
explanation.definitionFit: A maxim is a short pithy statement of a general truth.

clue.text: The girl from Westminster

parts.note: reads as a girl's name, but also as a set of initials for a wartime law passed by Parliament at Westminster

explanation.surface: Someone asks about a young woman from a London district.
explanation.walkthrough: DORA, the Defence of the Realm Act (1914), was a British wartime law, nicknamed as if it were a woman; Westminster is where Parliament sits.
explanation.definitionFit: The Defence of the Realm Act was nicknamed by its initials as though a woman, and it came from Parliament.

clue.text: Part of the hatter's stock-in-trade?

parts.note: a hatter sells headwear, and the Mad Hatter in Alice is a famously crazy one

explanation.surface: A question about what a milliner keeps in the shop.
explanation.walkthrough: A hatter would stock caps, and the Mad Hatter of Lewis Carroll would stock mad ones; the word also means a reckless person.
explanation.definitionFit: A reckless, impulsive person is called a madcap, punning on headwear for the Mad Hatter.

clue.text: They give the women's army inside information, as it were

indicators.note: inside says one piece sits within another here

parts.note: the ATS, Auxiliary Territorial Service, was the British women's army of the Second World War
gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: Spies feed secret intelligence to a women's military corps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inside information' reads as one phrase (secret knowledge passed to spies) but splits into a container signal and a slang word; the ATS dates the puzzle to the 1940s.
explanation.definitionFit: Spies and representatives are people who pass on secrets or act for others.

clue.text: A critic casts her distinctively

indicators.note: doing something distinctively means doing it in an individual way, here an individual arrangement of the letters

explanation.surface: A reviewer picks an actress for a part in an unusual way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'distinctively' rearranges A CRITIC CASTS HER; the whole clue also hints that distinctive traits are what a critic looks for.
explanation.definitionFit: Distinguishing traits are what mark out a person in a distinctive way.

clue.text: " For-she will prove a second Grissel " (T. of the Shrew)

definitions.text: " For-she will prove a second Grissel " (T. of the Shrew)

parts.words: " For-she will prove a second Grissel " (T. of the Shrew)
parts.note: a quotation from The Taming of the Shrew with one word missing after 'For'

explanation.surface: A line of Shakespeare quoted with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: Petruchio says of Katharina 'For patience she will prove a second Grissel'; Griselda was the proverbially long-suffering wife.
explanation.definitionFit: Griselda is the classic model of long-suffering endurance, the quality the missing word names.

clue.text: In the matter of alms the more she flags the more active she is

definitions.text: In the matter of alms the more she flags the more active she is

parts.words: In the matter of alms the more she flags the more active she is
parts.note: 'flags' seems to mean tires, but refers to selling paper flags on a charity flag day

explanation.surface: A paradox about a charity worker who works harder as she wilts.
explanation.walkthrough: On a British flag day, volunteers gave small paper flags to people who donated; the more she 'flags' (hands out flags), the busier she is.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman gathering charity money in the street is someone who gathers donations.

clue.text: Not necessarily meant by those who say "Look out, for squalls"

definitions.text: Not necessarily meant by those who say "Look out, for squalls"

parts.words: Not necessarily meant by those who say "Look out, for squalls"
parts.note: 'look out for squalls' is an idiom for expecting trouble, which need not be a prediction about the sky

explanation.surface: A remark that someone warning of trouble is not talking about the sky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look out for squalls' usually warns of a row or an angry outburst, so the speaker is not giving a meteorological prediction.
explanation.definitionFit: A prediction of rain, wind and sunshine is what squall warnings literally would be.

clue.text: Taken in church

parts.note: a priest is said to take holy ... when ordained, a ceremony held in church

explanation.surface: Something received during a church service, like communion.
explanation.walkthrough: One 'takes holy orders' when becoming a priest; the clue sounds like taking communion.
explanation.definitionFit: Ordination admits a person to the ranks of clergy, called holy orders.

clue.text: But it is not necessarily an uninteresting event

definitions.text: But it is not necessarily an uninteresting event

parts.words: But it is not necessarily an uninteresting event
parts.note: 'flat' can mean dull, but in horse racing a flat event is simply one without jumps

explanation.surface: Someone defends an occasion that sounds boring.
explanation.walkthrough: A flat race in horse racing has no fences; 'flat' meaning dull is the false trail.
explanation.definitionFit: Horse racing without hurdles or fences is called flat racing, a contest on level ground.

clue.text: Stone circles

parts.note: prehistoric rings or arrangements of standing stones

explanation.definitionFit: These are megalithic monuments, a term once used for rings of standing stones.

clue.text: Travellers should not lack accommodation in Austria

definitions.text: Travellers should not lack accommodation in Austria

parts.words: Travellers should not lack accommodation in Austria
parts.note: the city's name opens with 'inns', lodging for travellers, so a city that begins with inns should have plenty

explanation.surface: Advice for tourists that hotels in Austria are easy to find.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tyrolean city's name begins with INNS, places where travellers stay.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the capital of the Tyrol, a city in Austria whose name begins with lodgings.

clue.text: Nothing more than a convulsion

annotationWithheld.why: Nothing more than a convulsion (4): O + TIC gives the letters but no clue word defines 'relating to the ear'

clue.text: Dry Saxon (anag.)

annotationWithheld.why: Dry Saxon (anag.) (8): anagram fodder only, no clue word defines the gemstone

clue.text: But it doesn't require much effort to use it

definitions.text: But it doesn't require much effort to use it

parts.words: But it doesn't require much effort to use it
parts.note: to strain is to make a great effort, but also to pour liquid through a sieve

explanation.surface: A remark that some tool is easy to use despite its name.
explanation.walkthrough: The name suggests straining hard, yet pouring tea or vegetables through a sieve is effortless.
explanation.definitionFit: A sieve for draining liquids takes its name from the verb meaning to filter.

clue.text: A queer monocotyledon

parts.note: rum is old British slang for strange or odd

explanation.surface: A botanist calls a plant odd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'queer' here has its old sense of strange, which RUM also has in British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: The lily family relative called cuckoo-pint is a flowering plant with a single seed leaf.

clue.text: They don't " deliver the goods,"-on the contrary

definitions.text: They don't " deliver the goods,"-on the contrary

parts.words: They don't " deliver the goods,"-on the contrary
parts.note: 'deliver the goods' means succeed, but read literally the opposite of sending goods out is bringing them in

explanation.surface: A complaint about people who fail to live up to promises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deliver the goods' is an idiom for doing what was promised; these traders bring goods into the country instead of sending them.
explanation.definitionFit: Traders who bring foreign merchandise into a country are the opposite of exporters.

clue.text: The cure is, perhaps, in a sea-trip

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters of 'cure is' are one possible arrangement of another word

explanation.surface: A doctor suggests an ocean voyage as a remedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges CURE IS; the surface is the old prescription of a voyage for one's health.
explanation.definitionFit: A pleasure voyage by ship is a holiday at sea.

clue.text: The operatic character seems a temperate person

definitions.text: The operatic character seems a temperate person

parts.words: The operatic character seems a temperate person
parts.note: the hero's name splits into a phrase meaning a single glass of spirits, the order of a moderate drinker

explanation.surface: Someone notes that a figure in an opera is a moderate type.
explanation.walkthrough: Tchaikovsky's opera Eugene Onegin; split as ONE GIN, the name describes a drinker who stops at one.
explanation.definitionFit: Eugene Onegin is the title figure of Tchaikovsky's opera.

clue.text: Presumably he doesn't want to be of service

definitions.text: Presumably he doesn't want to be of service

parts.words: Presumably he doesn't want to be of service
parts.note: 'service' means military service, which a runaway soldier abandons

explanation.surface: A remark about someone unhelpful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of service' sounds like being helpful, but the service is the armed forces, which he has fled.
explanation.definitionFit: A soldier who abandons his unit without leave has run from military duty.

clue.text: Legal motor issue

parts.note: motor is British for a car
issue means offspring, so a son

explanation.surface: A dispute over a car that has gone to law.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Edward Carson was a celebrated barrister and judge, so 'Legal' stands for a legal figure.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Carson was a famous barrister who prosecuted Oscar Wilde, a great figure of the law.

clue.text: Manx weasel

annotationWithheld.why: Manx weasel (4): STOAT without its tail gives the letters but no clue word defines the portico

clue.text: Nevertheless devoid of status

parts.note: devoid of means without, broken into two words: not with
status means rank or standing

explanation.surface: Someone is described as nonetheless lacking rank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'devoid of status' is read as 'not with standing', which closes up into the conjunction.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean in spite of that, introducing a contrast.

clue.text: Defeated at Salamis

parts.note: Salamis was the sea battle of 480 BC where the Greeks beat the Persian fleet

explanation.surface: A line from a history book about a beaten commander.
explanation.definitionFit: The Persian king watched his navy lose to the Greeks in that battle.

clue.text: The military are using the organ, Sir

indicators.note: using suggests the letters of 'organ' and 'Sir' are put to work in another order

explanation.surface: Soldiers commandeer a church instrument and address someone politely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'using' rearranges ORGAN and SIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Troops stationed in a town or fort make up a military force.
